claude.sample_unit: patients (419 Karolinska, 438 VDB Matched, 1526 VDB Non-Matched)
models_evaluated: CNN (Lee et al.) for intraoperative hypotension prediction

links.outcome: AUC of CNN versus simple MAP threshold for predicting intraoperative hypotension across datasets
links.effect: CNN beat MAP threshold in the ambiguous Karolinska data (64.41 vs 61.92) but only marginally in VDB datasets (80.29 vs 78.46; 80.64 vs 79.80); threshold metrics were comparable at 80% specificity.
links.quote: In the Karolinska dataset, characterized by narrow class separation ( = 2.44 mmHg), the CNN model performed better than MAP threshold method (MAPthr), achieving a higher (64.41 vs. 61.92 ).

links.outcome: Performance inflation from selection bias excluding borderline MAP cases, tested by standardizing class separation
links.effect: Baseline AUCs differed (64.41 Karolinska vs ~80 VDB); after standardizing MAP difference to 5.01 mmHg, AUCs equalized (72.48, 71.79, 73.33), indicating selection bias inflated metrics.
links.quote: This standardization equalized performance ( for Karolinska, VDB Matched, and VDB Non-Matched), confirming that class separation bias inflates metrics in datasets with larger values (Table 5 ).

links.outcome: Cross-center and cross-cohort AUC when training on one site and testing on another
links.effect: Trained on VDB Matched, tested on Karolinska AUC fell to 63.25 (vs 80.29 within-site); VDB Non-Matched to Karolinska 63.76; Karolinska-trained models generalized to VDB at 68.28-70.62.
links.quote: Cross-center validation exposed asymmetric generalizability: models trained on Karolinska–with a larger Gray Zone prevalence ( 49 versus 18–20 in VDB datasets; see Fig. 3 , right panels)–generalized moderately to VDB Matched ( = 68.28 ), while the reverse (VDB Matched Karolinska) showed significant degradation ( = 63.25 ).

links.outcome: Performance degradation when applying models across datasets with different populations and class separation
links.effect: Models trained on well-separated VDB data degraded on Karolinska (AUC 63.25-63.76), while within-VDB transfer was consistent (79.16-80.63).
links.quote: These findings establish realistic expectations for AI-deployment in one hospital doesn’t guarantee success in another.

links.outcome: AUC across age groups and ASA classification subgroups
links.effect: AUC higher when tested on young cohort (~80-81) than old cohort (~75); restricting to ASA 2 gave comparable AUC to baseline (e.g., 62.93 vs 64.41 Karolinska).
links.quote: Finally, when restricting analysis to ASA class 2 only patients, the model maintained comparable performance to the baseline across all datasets ( ).

unlisted_practices: Including borderline (Gray Zone) cases and standardizing class separation to avoid selection bias in evaluation dataset construction
Poisson-based sampling with slack window to avoid label leakage in prediction framing

links.outcome: Predictive performance of CNN versus MAP threshold method across datasets
links.effect: In VDB cohorts, CNN was marginally better than MAPthr (AUC-ROC 80.29 vs 78.46, and 80.64 vs 79.80), but in Karolinska CNN was higher (64.41 vs 61.92); sensitivity, PPV, and F1 were comparable across all datasets.
links.quote: In contrast, for the VDB datasets–characterized by a wider class separation ( = 11.21–11.96 mmHg) and clearer hemodynamic patterns–the CNN model performed only marginally better than MAPthr ( = 80.29 vs. 78.46 for VDB Matched, and 80.64 vs. 79.80 for VDB Non-Matched).

links.outcome: Cross-center model generalizability and performance degradation from dataset shift
links.effect: Models trained on VDB Matched dropped to AUC-ROC 63.25 when tested on Karolinska (versus 80.29 internally), whereas Karolinska-trained models generalized to VDB Matched at AUC-ROC 68.28 (versus 64.41 internally).
